In the field of reinforcement learning, experience replay has been a crucial component that facilitates off-policy learning and improves the robustness of algorithms. However, the current implementation of experience replay has a major drawback: it randomly samples experiences from the replay buffer without considering their significance. This can lead to a significant waste of valuable data, as less informative experiences are repeatedly selected over more informative ones. To address this issue, we propose a novel experience replay method that dynamically adjusts the sampling probability of experiences based on their variance of returns. This approach ensures that experiences with higher variance are sampled more frequently, thereby accelerating the learning process. Our method, which we call Variance Decrease based Experience Replay (VDER), has been successfully applied to various policy gradient algorithms, including REINFORCE, Actor-Critic, and Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO). Experimental results demonstrate that VDER significantly improves the sample efficiency of these algorithms, with substantial gains in some cases. For instance, PPO with VDER achieves a 30% improvement in sample efficiency compared to the standard PPO algorithm. Moreover, VDER is computationally efficient and can be easily integrated into existing reinforcement learning frameworks. To facilitate the adoption of VDER, we have made our implementation publicly available on GitHub. This work provides a valuable contribution to the reinforcement learning community by offering a simple yet effective solution to improve the sample efficiency of off-policy learning algorithms. Additionally, the proposed method can be applied to other reinforcement learning algorithms to enhance their performance. Our code can be accessed at https://github.com/your-username/vder. Pretraining techniques for natural language processing have achieved significant success
in multiple areas, but existing methods have limitations. Specifically, they either
rely on bidirectional contextualization or assume full access to the input sequence,
which is not always feasible. To overcome these challenges, we introduce XLNet, a
pretraining approach that combines the benefits of autoregressive and autoregressive-
free pretraining methods. By using enhanced permutation APIs, XLNet can capture
long-range contextual dependencies without relying on the full input sequence. 
Experimental results show that XLNet surpasses previous state-of-the-art methods on
13 out of 19 tasks, including GLUE and SuperGLUE benchmarks, while also achieving
state-of-the-art performance on SQuAD v1.1 and v1.2. Notably, XLNet's performance
is achieved with significantly fewer parameters than BERT-Large. Moreover, XLNet's
pretrained models can be fine-tuned for multiple downstream tasks without further
pretraining, which is a significant advantage. To facilitate further research, we
release XLNet's code and pre-trained models at https://github.com/yingkaiping/xlnet.

domains.  Experimental results demonstrate that Dict-BERT outperforms existing
models, achieving a 2.1% improvement in F1 score on the MedQA dataset.  Our code
is publicly available at https://github.com/zhengyuan-yu/Dict-BERT.

distinguishing between genuine and fabricated news headlines, with a focus on
those generated through automatic processes. We introduce a novel dataset,
HeadFake, comprising 10,000 human-created and 10,000 artificially produced
headlines, with accompanying articles and labels indicating authenticity.
Our experiments reveal that a BERT-based model achieves a 74.5% accuracy rate in
identifying fabricated headlines, with a 4% improvement over a comparable
LSTM-based model. Notably, our results indicate that a BERT-based model
performs better when trained on artificially produced headlines compared to
human-created ones. This counterintuitive finding suggests that machine-
generated text may serve as a more effective training signal for NLP models. 
Moreover, our analysis reveals that a BERT-based model is more susceptible
to adversarial attacks when trained on human-created data, with a 10% accuracy
drop when subjected to a 10% alteration in input text. Conversely, our
results indicate that a BERT-based model is more resilient to adversarial
attacks when trained on artificially produced headlines, with a 5% accuracy
drop when subjected to a 10% alteration in input text. Our study provides
insights into the potential applications of NLP models in detecting fabricated
news headlines and highlights the importance of considering the source of

In neural networks, the extent of synaptic connections between neurons plays a crucial role in information transmission. This study examines the effects of varying extent distributions on the dynamics of random networks composed of leaky integrate-and-fire neurons. By adjusting the extent of connections, we observe changes in the network's behavior, including the emergence of synchronized activity and chaotic dynamics. Our findings reveal that the extent distribution significantly influences the network's behavior, and we provide a mathematical explanation for these results. Additionally, we investigate the effects of heterogeneity in neuron parameters and synapse strength on the network's dynamics. Our research provides insights into the design of artificial neural networks and sheds light on the underlying mechanisms of biological neural systems. This study is a precursor to investigating more complex networks, such as those with directed connections, and we discuss potential avenues for future research. In action detection, the goal is to identify actions within videos without explicit temporal and spatial annotations. Current approaches rely on pre-trained models that recognize actions based on predefined features, but these features are insufficient for identifying actions in complex scenarios. To address this limitation, we propose a novel method that leverages graph convolutions to learn context from spatial features, allowing for more accurate action detection. Our approach, called Spot What Counts, involves a two-stage process: first, we identify key frames that contain the action, and second, we use graph convolutions to learn context from these frames and predict action boundaries. Our method outperforms state-of-the-art approaches on the JHMDB and UCF101 datasets, achieving a significant improvement of 4.5% mAP on JHMDB and 2.5% mAP on UCF101. Our code is available at https://github.com/zhengyuzhang/SWAC.

novel approach to pretraining, combining image and text modalities with 
additional guidance from product attributes to improve multimodal representation 
learning. This method, called IRIS, incorporates attribute recognition to 
facilitate multimodal pretraining, which is then applied to product image 
recognition tasks. Experiments on two datasets demonstrate the superiority of 
IRIS over existing methods in product image classification and retrieval tasks.

method is also applied to a product image captioning task, yielding 
state-of-the-art results. The proposed approach is made available to the

Continual Learning (CL) poses significant challenges to machine learning models as they must adapt to new tasks without compromising their performance on previous ones. A novel approach, Online Collective Continual Learning (OCLL), has been developed to address this issue by aggregating multiple neural networks, each trained on a single task, to mitigate catastrophic forgetting. By leveraging a shared neural network, OCLL achieves a seamless integration of new tasks without requiring explicit regularization techniques. Through extensive experimentation, OCLL demonstrates superior performance across various benchmarks, including image classification and language modeling, by effectively retaining knowledge from previous tasks. Furthermore, OCLL's architecture is designed to facilitate efficient online learning, allowing it to be trained incrementally without requiring access to all previous data. By decoupling task aggregation from individual training, OCLL provides a flexible framework for CL applications. Notably, OCLL's architecture is modular and can be easily adapted to different scenarios, including both online and offline settings. A key advantage of OCLL is its ability to accommodate a large number of tasks, with the ability to scale up to 100 tasks without compromising performance. By analyzing the model's behavior, it is observed that OCLL's task aggregation mechanism effectively reduces forgetting by adapting to task similarities and differences. A thorough analysis of OCLL's architecture and its components is also provided, shedding light on its behavior and its potential applications. The availability of large-scale datasets with precise bounding-box annotations has significantly contributed to advancements in this area. 
However, the process of manually annotating images is labor-intensive and costly, limiting the scope of datasets that can be developed. 
To address this issue, we introduce a novel method for creating a large-scale dataset of images containing various objects, without the need for manual bounding-box annotations. 
Our approach involves utilizing a pre-trained object detector to generate pseudo-annotations for a large collection of images, which are then used to train a more advanced object detector.

A major challenge in multiple sclerosis (MS) research is developing automated lesion segmentation that can be applied across various clinics. Current solutions often rely on datasets from a single institution, which can lead to overfitting and limited generalizability. This study investigates whether training models on multiple datasets simultaneously can improve their performance on unseen data compared to training on a single dataset or from scratch. We conducted a comprehensive analysis using 11 public datasets from 8 clinics, comparing the performance of models trained on individual datasets, multiple datasets simultaneously, and from scratch. This suggests that training on multiple datasets simultaneously is a valuable strategy for developing robust MS lesion segmentation models. Recent advancements in language models have led to significant performance improvements
in various NLP tasks, but they come with substantial computational costs. To address
this issue, researchers have been exploring more efficient methods, such as parameter-
efficient fine-tuning, which can be applied to smaller models. However, these methods
still require a large number of parameters to be adjusted, which can be impractical.
To overcome this limitation, we propose a new approach called Unique Token Adaptation
(UTA), which allows for the adjustment of a tiny fraction of parameters, specifically
those associated with unique tokens, to adapt a pre-trained model to a specific task.
Our experiments demonstrate that UTA can achieve comparable results to full fine-tuning
with significantly fewer parameters adjusted, and even outperform it in some cases by
reducing overfitting. Our findings suggest that UTA can be a valuable tool for efficient
model adaptation in NLP. Our code is available at https://github.com/DeepLearnApps/UTA.
